parts.title: A repair café in town
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When a toaster stopped working, I nearly put it in the bin. Then my neighbour told me about the repair café at the community centre. It opens one Saturday a month, and volunteers help visitors repair small household objects. I was unsure whether I could fix anything, but the volunteer showed me how to test the cable safely. The toaster worked again after ten minutes.

The café is not a shop, and the volunteers do not promise that every object can be repaired. People bring old lamps, toys and clothes, and they learn by watching or helping. Last month, a retired electrician taught two teenagers how to replace a plug. They came back this week with a radio they had repaired at home.

My favourite part is the friendly atmosphere. Visitors can have tea while they wait, and someone usually brings a cake. The project also has a practical benefit: fewer things are thrown away. The organisers hope to open on two Saturdays each month, but they need more volunteers before they can do that.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer visit the repair café?
options: The community centre was selling kitchen equipment.
The writer wanted to repair a toaster.
The writer wanted to meet the volunteers.
questions.explanation: Her toaster stopped working and a neighbour told her about the café, so she went there to repair the toaster.

questions.prompt: What did the volunteer do first?
options: Replaced the toaster with another one.
Explained how to test the cable safely.
Asked the writer to buy a new tool.
Brought the writer a cup of tea.
questions.explanation: The volunteer showed her how to test the cable safely, and then the toaster worked again.

questions.prompt: What happened to the two teenagers?
options: They opened a repair café at home.
They were given a prize by the volunteers.
They returned after repairing a radio themselves.
questions.explanation: The teenagers came back this week with a radio they had repaired at home.

questions.prompt: What does the writer like about the café?
options: It gives free tools to everyone.
questions.explanation: Her favourite part is the friendly atmosphere, which means it is welcoming.

questions.prompt: What do the organisers need before opening more often?
options: Raise money for a new building.
questions.explanation: They need more volunteers, which means additional helpers, before they can open two Saturdays a month.

parts.title: A new cycle route
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage: Last year, the town council asked residents how to make short journeys easier. [1] Many people said they would cycle if they felt safer near the busy shopping street. [2] The council painted a cycle lane and added signs at both ends. Work began in March, just before the weather became warmer. [3] During the first week, volunteers stood nearby and explained how to use the new route. They also asked cyclists to report any problems. [4] One corner was difficult to see, so the council moved a small sign. Since then, more parents have used the route to take their children to school. [5] The council now plans to connect it to the railway station.
sentences: That feedback helped the council make a small improvement.
This quick change made the crossing clearer.
The new bus lane opened two months later.
The most common suggestion was a protected route into the centre.
In response, they planned a route away from the main road.
Local cyclists were invited to test the lane when it opened.
Many shops on that street are closed on Sundays.
The council is also offering free bicycle lessons next month.

gaps.explanation: “The most common suggestion was a protected route” follows the council asking residents and is followed by what many people said.
“In response, they planned a route away from the main road” answers the residents’ worry about the busy shopping street.
“Local cyclists were invited to test the lane” follows the work and leads to what happened in the first week.
“That feedback helped the council make a small improvement” follows cyclists reporting problems and leads to the moved sign.
“The council is also offering free bicycle lessons” follows the parents using the route and leads to the next plan. Sentence D would only fit straight after the sign was moved.

parts.title: Getting around without a car
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word or phrase for each gap.
parts.passage: More people in our town are choosing to [1] the bus to work. A new travel app makes it easier to [2] when buses arrive. The council has also [3] a lower price for weekly tickets. Some people still find the bus [4] at busy times, so extra services will start next month. If the plan is successful, there may be [5] cars on the road and the air could be much [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: We take the bus; do, make and go do not combine with “the bus” in this way.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: You check when buses arrive using an app.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: A council introduces a lower price; the other verbs do not fit.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: At busy times a bus is crowded, which means full of people.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: We use “fewer” with countable plural nouns such as cars.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: “Much cleaner” is the comparative form after “much”.

parts.title: A shared garden
parts.instructions: Complete the text with one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Our street has a small garden [1] to the library. It was empty [2] several years, so local people decided to use it. Everyone can help, even [3] they have only a little time. We usually meet [4] Saturday morning and share the jobs. Some neighbours grow flowers, [5] others look after the vegetables. We hope the garden will become a place [6] people can relax together.

gaps.explanation: Next to the library means beside it.
We say “empty for several years” to show how long.
“Even if they have only a little time” means although it is possible that they do.
We use “on” with days: on Saturday morning.
“While” contrasts what two groups of neighbours do.
“Where” refers to the place and begins the clause about relaxing there.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: peter
turns.text: Ready to go? Have you got everything?

turns.speaker: alina
turns.text: Let me check. Phone, yes. I nearly left it on the table, but it’s in my bag now.

turns.speaker: peter
turns.text: And it’s cold outside. Coat?

turns.speaker: alina
turns.text: I’m wearing it, can’t you see? Oh no, the bus pass! I left it on the kitchen shelf.

turns.speaker: peter
turns.text: The monthly one? Do you want to go back for it?

turns.speaker: alina
turns.text: There isn’t time. I’ll buy a single ticket from the driver. Come on, or we’ll miss the bus.

question.explanation: Alina has her phone in her bag and is wearing her coat, but she left her bus pass at home, so she must buy a ticket from the driver.

turns.speaker: rob
turns.text: What’s the plan for Saturday, Tessa? Are we starting with the flowers?

turns.speaker: tessa
turns.text: That’s the last job, in the afternoon, once the ground is ready. The fence comes after lunch.

turns.speaker: rob
turns.text: So what are we doing first?

turns.speaker: tessa
turns.text: Rubbish. The path by the river is full of bottles and bags, and we can’t plant anything until it’s clean.

turns.speaker: rob
turns.text: Okay. Gloves and bin bags, then. Where do we meet?

turns.speaker: tessa
turns.text: At the bridge at nine. Bring a hat.

question.prompt: What will the volunteers do first?
question.explanation: Flowers are the last job and the fence comes after lunch; the first job is picking up the rubbish so that the river path is clean.

turns.speaker: mei
turns.text: Are you off out, Idris? I thought you were meeting Sam today.

turns.speaker: idris
turns.text: That’s tomorrow. Today I’m taking my bicycle to the shop on Dale Street.

turns.speaker: mei
turns.text: To buy a bus pass? You said that cycling was too tiring in winter.

turns.speaker: idris
turns.text: I thought about it, but the pass costs forty pounds a month. No, the back wheel is bent since I hit that kerb. The man says he can do the repair by lunchtime.

turns.speaker: mei
turns.text: Good. Can you bring me some milk on the way back?

question.prompt: Why is the cyclist going to the shop?
question.explanation: Idris is not meeting Sam until tomorrow and decided against the expensive bus pass; the shop will do the repair of his bent wheel.

turns.speaker: stefan
turns.text: Joan, I saw your car outside the garage on Elm Road. Is it broken?

turns.speaker: joan
turns.text: It’s being serviced, so I can’t drive today. I thought about my bicycle, but it’s pouring.

turns.speaker: stefan
turns.text: So how will you get to work?

turns.speaker: joan
turns.text: The same as last Tuesday. The quarter past eight from Bridge Street, then a ten-minute walk.

turns.speaker: stefan
turns.text: Last Tuesday you said it was too crowded.

turns.speaker: joan
turns.text: It was packed, but at least the train is reliable. Better than getting wet.

question.prompt: How does the woman travel today?
question.explanation: Her car is at the garage and it is too wet to cycle, so she will take the quarter past eight from Bridge Street, which is the train.

turns.speaker: hassan
turns.text: Would you like to look at these shopping bags?

turns.speaker: poppy
turns.text: They look nice. Do they keep things cold? I need something for the picnic.

turns.speaker: hassan
turns.text: No, that would be a different kind, with a lining. These are just cotton.

turns.speaker: poppy
turns.text: Are they made by hand? The sign says "handmade" on the other table.

turns.speaker: hassan
turns.text: Those ones are, and they cost twice as much. These come from a factory. But look, you fold it into a little square and slip it into your pocket.

turns.speaker: poppy
turns.text: Oh, clever. I’ll take three.

question.prompt: What is special about the bags?
options: They are easy to carry in a pocket.
question.explanation: The bags are not cold bags and are not handmade; the special thing is that they fold into a small square that fits into a pocket.

turns.speaker: gwen
turns.text: Shall we eat at home tonight? I could cook pasta.

turns.speaker: callum
turns.text: I’d love that, but the fridge is empty. What about the park? A picnic?

turns.speaker: gwen
turns.text: It’s going to rain after five.

turns.speaker: callum
turns.text: True. How about that little place on the corner, with the blue door?

turns.speaker: gwen
turns.text: The café that serves good soup? Yes! They’re open until nine.

turns.speaker: callum
turns.text: I’ll book a table for seven, and I’ll ask for the one by the window. Do you want me to meet you there, or shall we walk together from your flat?

turns.speaker: gwen
turns.text: Let’s walk. I need some fresh air after sitting at the computer all day.

question.explanation: Home has no food and the park will be wet, so they choose the little café on the corner with the blue door.

turns.speaker: ewan
turns.text: Did you use the new crossing by the station, Dot?

turns.speaker: dot
turns.text: Yes. It’s well lit, so I’d feel fine there even at night, and it isn’t difficult to find. The signs are big. You can’t miss it.

turns.speaker: ewan
turns.text: So what do you think of it?

turns.speaker: dot
turns.text: Honestly, it’s very useful, because the road was so dangerous before. But the lights take forever to change. I waited nearly two minutes this morning.

turns.speaker: ewan
turns.text: That’s long.

turns.speaker: dot
turns.text: It is, but it’s better than nothing.

question.prompt: What does the woman think about the crossing?
question.explanation: Dot says it is well lit and easy to see, and she calls it very useful, but she complains that the lights take forever to change.

parts.title: Everyday conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to each conversation and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: nell
turns.text: Did you hear? The driver says the main road is closed for repairs, so we’ll go round through the villages.

turns.speaker: barry
turns.text: That adds about forty minutes, I think.

turns.speaker: nell
turns.text: Will you miss your train?

turns.speaker: barry
turns.text: No, mine isn’t until six, and it’s only three. I’ve got plenty of time. Actually, it’s a bonus. I like seeing the villages.

turns.speaker: nell
turns.text: I thought you’d be annoyed. Last time you shouted at the driver.

turns.speaker: barry
turns.text: That was because he was rude. Today he’s been fine.

turns.speaker: nell
turns.text: Well, I’m happy if you’re happy.

question.prompt: How does Barry feel about the longer journey?
question.explanation: Barry says his train is not until six and he likes seeing the villages, and the driver today has been fine, so he is relaxed.

turns.speaker: ola
turns.text: The market closes at six today, doesn’t it?

turns.speaker: kurt
turns.text: Yes, but the fish stalls pack up earlier, around four, and we need fish for the dinner.

turns.speaker: ola
turns.text: Can’t we go tomorrow morning instead?

turns.speaker: kurt
turns.text: The guests arrive at eleven, and I want to cook before they come. It has to be today.

turns.speaker: ola
turns.text: I’ve got a meeting until half past three, and then I have to pick up the flowers from my sister’s house.

turns.speaker: kurt
turns.text: Then run. I’ll meet you at the entrance at ten to four.

question.prompt: What do Ola and Kurt agree to do?
options: Go to the market before six today
Go to the market tomorrow morning
Go to the market before four today
question.explanation: The market closes at six, but the fish stalls pack up at four and tomorrow morning is too late, so they plan to meet at ten to four.

turns.speaker: glen
turns.text: I sent the plan for Saturday’s journey by email, but nobody replied.

turns.speaker: fay
turns.text: People never read them. Another email wouldn’t help.

turns.speaker: glen
turns.text: Should I change the journey, then? Take a shorter route?

turns.speaker: fay
turns.text: No, the route is fine. The problem is that nobody can open the file on a phone. Why don’t you make paper copies and hand them out at the meeting on Thursday?

turns.speaker: glen
turns.text: That’s a good idea.

turns.speaker: fay
turns.text: It costs pennies on the office printer.

question.prompt: What does Fay advise Glen to do?
question.explanation: Fay says a second email would not help and the route is fine, so she suggests giving out paper copies of the plan at the Thursday meeting.

turns.speaker: vic
turns.text: The concert starts at eight. A taxi from here costs about twenty pounds.

turns.speaker: una
turns.text: Too much. We could walk. It’s about an hour.

turns.speaker: vic
turns.text: In these shoes? No, my feet already hurt, and it’ll be dark by the time we come back.

turns.speaker: una
turns.text: The number fourteen stops outside the hall, doesn’t it?

turns.speaker: vic
turns.text: Every ten minutes until eleven, and only three pounds.

turns.speaker: una
turns.text: Settled, then. I’ll get the cash from the machine on the way, and we can leave at half past seven.

turns.speaker: vic
turns.text: Perfect. I’ll meet you at the corner. Don’t be late this time.

question.prompt: How do Vic and Una decide to get to the concert?
question.explanation: A taxi costs twenty pounds and a walk of an hour in the dark is a bad idea, so they take the number fourteen, which stops outside the hall.

turns.speaker: mo
turns.text: I’m off to the airport. Can you do a few things while I’m away?

turns.speaker: cora
turns.text: Sure. Water the plants?

turns.speaker: mo
turns.text: Yes, but that’s Thursday. Before you go to work tomorrow, can you check the light in the hall? I always leave it on, and it uses a lot of electricity.

turns.speaker: cora
turns.text: Fine. What about the windows? It gets very hot in the flat when the sun comes in.

turns.speaker: mo
turns.text: I closed them all, and the neighbour’s cat can’t get in. And the gate is locked, I did it already. The spare key is under the blue pot if you need it.

turns.speaker: cora
turns.text: Great. Have a good flight, and send me a message when you land.

question.prompt: What does Mo ask Cora to do?
question.explanation: Mo says the windows are closed and the gate is locked; his request is that Cora checks the hall light, which he always leaves on.

turns.speaker: dan
turns.text: Come in, sit down. You look cold. Tea? I’ve got milk and sugar.

turns.speaker: rhea
turns.text: Not milk, thanks. It upsets my stomach. And I stopped taking sugar in January.

turns.speaker: dan
turns.text: Oh. I could find some honey.

turns.speaker: rhea
turns.text: No, thank you, I’m trying not to eat sweet things, even in the afternoon. But is there a lemon in the fridge? One slice is perfect.

turns.speaker: dan
turns.text: There’s half of one. Coming up. Would you like a biscuit? I made them this morning, but they’re a bit burnt.

turns.speaker: rhea
turns.text: Why not? I like them burnt.

question.prompt: What does Rhea want in her tea?
question.explanation: Rhea refuses milk, sugar and honey, but asks for a slice from the lemon in the fridge.

parts.title: A town clean-up day
parts.instructions: Listen and complete the notes. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time in each gap.

turns.speaker: gemma
turns.text: Hello, everyone. I’m Gemma, and I’m organising our town clean-up day. Thank you for coming to this meeting. First, the place. In the past, we always met at the town hall, but it’s closed for repairs, so this time we will meet at the library. You’ll see me at the front door with a yellow flag. We start at nine o’clock. I know some people hoped for ten, but the rubbish lorry comes at ten, and we want to fill it. Now, what to wear? Please wear old clothes. We’ll be touching dirty things all day, so choose something that you don’t mind losing. Strong shoes are also a good idea, but we have plenty of gloves for everyone. Let me explain the work. The first group will pick up rubbish in the main street and along the canal. The second group will do some painting. Last year we painted the school wall, and everyone loved it. This year the job is the benches in the park, which are in a terrible state. We have the paint and brushes, but not enough overalls, so bring an apron if you have one. It will be a warm day, so bring a bottle of water. Don’t worry about juice or other drinks, because the café will give them out all day, but the water in the park fountain is not drinkable. At one o’clock, we all stop for lunch. We asked the school kitchen first, but they are closed on Saturdays, so the café is providing the sandwiches and fruit. They are being very kind, so please thank them. We finish at four, and the mayor will come to say hello. Thank you, and see you on Saturday.

gaps.prompt: Meeting point (not the town hall): the ___
gaps.explanation: She says they used to meet at the town hall, but this time they meet at the library.

gaps.prompt: The work starts at ___ o'clock in the morning
gaps.explanation: She says they start at nine; ten is when the rubbish lorry comes.

gaps.prompt: Dress code: ___ that you don't mind getting dirty
gaps.explanation: She says to wear old clothes that you don’t mind losing; strong shoes are only a good idea.

gaps.prompt: The painting job this year is the park ___
gaps.explanation: Last year they painted the school wall, but this year the job is the benches in the park.
She says to bring a bottle of water because the fountain water is not drinkable; the café gives out other drinks.

gaps.prompt: The sandwiches and fruit come from the ___
gaps.explanation: The school kitchen is closed on Saturdays, so the café is providing the sandwiches and fruit.

parts.title: An interview with a town planner
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Gareth, you’re a town planner. What first made you interested in the job?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: Funny story. As a teenager I worked in my uncle’s shop on Saturdays, and I enjoyed it, but I didn’t think about the street outside. Later they built a new hospital in our town, and everybody talked about it, but it wasn’t the hospital that interested me. It was the small square outside my school, which was just a car park until the council turned it into a place for benches and trees. I wanted to do that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And what are you working on now?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: I’m not building a shopping centre, thank goodness, and the school has already been built. My current project is about the route to the hospital. At the moment people on foot and on bicycles have to cross a very busy road, and some of them are afraid of it. So I’m trying to make that route safer, with a new crossing and wider paths.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Is it going well?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: Mostly, but there’s one big problem. The road isn’t too far away from the hospital, and residents do use it, as you’d expect. The difficulty is that in the morning the traffic is heavy for about two hours, and any change we make has to work then. It’s hard to test ideas when the road is full of cars and buses.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why do you talk to shop owners?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: People think I only meet residents, but shop owners have been there for twenty years, and they know how an area changes. They notice when a street gets busier or when customers stop coming. They aren’t in charge of choosing trees, and the residents’ meetings are organised by the council. But their knowledge is really valuable.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you enjoy most about your work?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: I like making maps, and I enjoy presenting them to the council, though I get nervous. And finishing quickly is almost never possible in my job. The real pleasure is going back a year later and seeing families using a place that we improved. That makes the long meetings worth it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young planner?

turns.speaker: gareth
turns.text: Talk to residents. Don’t avoid questions, even difficult ones. I don’t think you need a degree in business, although it can help. The most important thing is to listen carefully, and then explain your ideas clearly, without long words, so that everybody understands.

questions.prompt: What first interested Gareth in town planning?
options: Improving a square near a school
questions.explanation: Gareth says it was not his uncle’s shop or the new hospital; the small square outside his school became a place for benches and trees, and he wanted to do that.

questions.prompt: What is Gareth working on now?
questions.explanation: He is not working on a shopping centre or a school; his current project is making the route to the hospital safer.

questions.prompt: What is the main difficulty with this project?
options: The road is too far away.
Residents do not use the hospital.
questions.explanation: The road is not too far and residents do use the hospital; the difficulty is that the morning traffic is heavy for about two hours.

questions.prompt: Why does Gareth talk to shop owners?
options: They know how the area changes.
questions.explanation: Shop owners have been there for twenty years and know how an area changes; they do not choose trees or organise meetings.

questions.prompt: What does Gareth enjoy most?
questions.explanation: He likes maps and presenting but the real pleasure is going back a year later and seeing families using an improved place.

questions.prompt: What advice does Gareth give?
questions.explanation: He says not to avoid questions and that a business degree is not necessary; the most important thing is to listen carefully and explain ideas clearly.
